newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Gold sets the pace among commodities.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Gold sets the pace among commodities.

text.p: Several key commodities including wheat and oil firmed at week's end but couldn't match a brisk pace set by the precious metals.
Gold rallied to its highest London fixing for five weeks on Friday and palladium caught the spotlight again as it fixed at a two-year high of $164.50 an ounce, up from Thursday's finish at $158.90.
Spot gold fixed at $345.85 an ounce, the highest since April 14 and up $2.20 from Thursday.
But dealers weren't convinced gold was headed for a big rally after languishing for some time because of sales by some central banks.
"I think it's just a reflection of physical demand that is clearly going on, and it caught the market a little bit short," said one dealer.
This, as well as illiquidity in platinum and palladium markets as a result of delays in Russian shipments, suddenly boosted prospects across the precious metals sector.
Gold had been stuck between $339-$343 since mid-April in a market cowed by the threat of selling by central banks and other institutions.
Some dealers say sellers are waiting to ambush gold again above $350.
London Metal Exchange (LME) base metals consolidated after gains earlier in the week.
Zinc was the star on Thursday when it reached 4-1/2 year highs of $1,328 per tonne. It was little changed during Friday.

It is up some 25 percent this year. Used in galvanising steel and manufacturing brass, it became the darling of funds and speculators in recent months after world demand overtook production and started eating into big inventories.
Unsettled weather again buoyed benchmark world wheat prices on the Chicago Board of Trade.
July futures were soon up five cents at $4.14 per bushel after temperatures dropped below freezing overnight in Nebraska and Kansas wheat growing areas, traders said.
Wheat was further bolstered by some long-term forecasts that showed warm and dry conditions would prevail in western Kansas. Soil is already dry there, crop scouts have said.
Crude oil prices were firm despite scepticism on the ability of members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries, meeting in Iran, to curb violations of their output quotas.
"I simply don't believe it," veteran OPEC watcher Mehdi Varzi of Kleinwort Benson told Reuters in Isfahan. "I would be amazed if the likes of Venezuela reined back output".
Continued excess may mean that prices, down more than $6 at $18 a barrel this year for the benchmark Brent Blend, could fall further, said the OPEC secretary-general, Rilwanu Lukman of Nigeria.
Friday, however, saw some modest firming of the price, with Brent trading as high as $18.87 on prospects of tighter short-term supply from the North Sea.

Coffee prices, after advancing again earlier in the week, were flat to easier on light selling. London July futures for robusta coffee beans hit a six-week high of $1,785 per tonne on Thursday but closed Friday lower at $1,758.
